title: Shrewsbury biscuits
subtitle: classic British butter biscuits with currants
excerpt: Shrewsbury biscuits are a classic British rolled biscuit made with butter, sugar, egg, and currants. You get a round, lightly crisp biscuit with a clean lemon flavour from the zest. Watch the baking time: a minute too long and they lose their tender centre.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton (Book of Household Management, 1861, public domain). Traditional Shrewsbury recipe documented in various 18th and 19th century British baking manuals.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked biscuits in a single layer, then store in a bag for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature for 20 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the recipe and freeze half the baked biscuits.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be wrapped and refrigerated for up to 2 days before rolling. Baked biscuits keep in an airtight tin for 5 days.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 180 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 165 degrees Celsius. Middle shelf.

glossaryTerms.definition: A biscuit dough with a high ratio of fat to flour, which gives a crumbly, melt-in-the-mouth texture rather than a chewy one. The fat coats the flour particles and inhibits gluten development. Shrewsbury biscuits fall into this family: they are enriched with egg as well as butter, which makes them slightly less crumbly than a pure shortbread.

Chilling a biscuit or pastry dough in the refrigerator before rolling. The rest firms the fat, which makes the dough easier to handle without sticking, and relaxes any gluten that formed during mixing so the biscuits do not shrink back during baking.

Rolling butter biscuit dough to an even thickness so the biscuits bake uniformly. The standard thickness for Shrewsbury biscuits is about 5 mm. Use a light touch: pressing too hard compresses the dough and makes the surface uneven.

Beat the softened butter and caster sugar together until pale and fluffy. Beat in the egg and lemon zest, and the rose water if using. The mixture may look slightly curdled at this point; that is fine.
Sift in the flour and stir until a soft dough forms. Fold in the currants. This is a
: it should be soft but not sticky. If it is very sticky, add a little extra flour, one teaspoon at a time.
Flatten the dough into a disc, wrap in baking paper or cling film, and refrigerate for 30 minutes. This
step firms the butter so the dough rolls cleanly.
Preheat the oven to 180 degrees Celsius. Line two baking trays with baking paper.

Gather the scraps, re-roll once, and cut more rounds. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the edges are just turning pale gold and the centres still look soft. Remove from the oven; the centres will firm as they cool. Transfer to a cooling rack after 5 minutes.

attrs.problem: The dough is too sticky to roll
attrs.avoid: Avoid rolling the dough straight from the mixing bowl without chilling.
attrs.fix: Return the dough to the fridge for a further 15 to 20 minutes. If it is still very sticky after chilling, the butter was too warm when you mixed it. Dust the work surface lightly with flour and roll quickly.

attrs.problem: The biscuits spread and lose their shape in the oven
attrs.avoid: Avoid placing biscuits on warm trays straight from a previous batch.
attrs.fix: Ensure the trays are cool before loading. If the biscuits spread significantly, the butter was too soft or the dough was not chilled long enough. Chill the cut biscuits on the tray for 10 minutes before baking next time.

attrs.problem: The biscuits are hard rather than tender
attrs.avoid: Avoid overbaking: these biscuits continue to firm as they cool on the tray.
attrs.fix: Remove from the oven when the edges are just beginning to colour and the centres look underdone. They will firm to the correct texture within 5 minutes of coming out of the oven.
